name: How to Freeze and Defrost Pizza Dough
description: Vito Iacopelli's method for freezing leftover pizza dough at its peak and defrosting it so it bakes like fresh, keeping well for about three to four months.

itemListElement.text: Use the dough at its correct point of fermentation, the same point at which you would bake with it, not over-proofed and not under-proofed.
Wrap the dough tightly so there is no air trapped inside.
Lay the wrapped dough flat in the freezer (keep the surface flat, do not let it fold or curl) and freeze until solid.
After about 24 hours, once the dough is completely frozen, peel off the plastic wrap. Work quickly so the dough does not start to defrost.
Detach the frozen dough balls from each other.
Wrap each dough ball individually and return them to the freezer; this saves space and keeps them well for about three to four months (longer if you remove all the air).

The night before you want to bake, put a little semolina (or flour) on the bottom of a pan, place a frozen dough ball in, dust the top with more semolina so the cover will not stick, cover, and put it in the fridge overnight.
The next morning, take the dough out of the fridge; the slow overnight thaw brings it back to life, soft and ready.
Take the dough out of the fridge about 1 hour before using so it comes to room temperature (this avoids black spots on the baked pizza). Keep any dough you are not using covered.
Dust with semolina, stretch the base (keep it to about 10 inches if the dough is highly hydrated), and pop any large bubbles so they do not scorch.
Top and bake as usual; the crust comes out like fresh dough.
